To critique a statement means to point out its strengths or its faults.
Zayyafa al-dirham means to reject or devalue a coin as counterfeit.
Rasafa al-ḥijāra means to fit stones tightly together.
Shadhdha al-sikkīn means to sharpen a knife or similar tool.
Talaqqafa al-shayʾ means to catch or take something quickly.

A journey is movement away from one's home or present place toward a goal, crossing stages and stopping places. There is an outward journey, which needs no explanation, and an inward journey. Those who know through direct experience describe four inward journeys.

The first journey is from creation to God. The traveler lifts the dark and luminous veils between themselves and their own deepest reality, which has always been with them. Put another way, the traveler rises from the level of the self to the heart, from the heart to the spirit, and from the spirit to the highest goal and greatest joy: the Garden brought near to those who are mindful of God.

The stains of the self are dark veils. The lights of the heart and the radiance of the spirit are luminous veils. These are the three main levels of the human being. The saying that a thousand veils stand between the servant and the Lord refers to these three broad levels. When the traveler reaches the goal by lifting these veils, they behold the beauty of the Real and their separate self disappears in Him. This may be called “the loss of the separate self in God’s Essence.” The secret, the hidden, and the most hidden belong here too, but they are also discussed in connection with the second journey.

The level of the spirit may be divided further by including the intellect, since it gives a more detailed account of the realities that can be known. The seven levels then become the self, the heart, the intellect, the spirit, the secret, the hidden, and the most hidden. These names apply when the traveler has reached a lasting spiritual state. Without that stability, they are not stations. They are the levels of spiritual friendship and the lands of love that Rumi refers to:
Attar has crossed the seven cities of love; we are still at the bend of a single alley.

When the traveler's separate self disappears in God, the first journey ends. Their existence is then through God. They enter a state in which their separate self fades away and may speak in ecstatic words for which people judge them an unbeliever and impose a penalty.

If divine care comes to their aid, that state passes. Clear awareness returns, and they admit their own error and servanthood after having spoken as if they shared in lordship. Abū Yazīd al-Bisṭāmī is reported to have said: “My God, if I ever say, ‘Glory be to me! How great is my majesty!’ then I am a Zoroastrian unbeliever. Break my sacred girdle, and I declare: There is no god but God, and Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.” Perhaps this discussion has already gone beyond its purpose. If it were not tiring to speak at length and tiring to listen, I would say much more about this journey. What I have set out is enough for now.

When the first journey ends, the traveler begins the second: from God to God, through God. It takes place through God because the traveler has become a saint whose existence is through God. The traveler moves from the station of the divine Essence through its perfections, one by one, until seeing all the divine qualities except those God has kept to Himself. Their sainthood is complete. Their own essence, actions, and qualities are understood through God's essence, actions, and qualities: through Him they hear, see, walk, and act.

The “secret” is when the separate self disappears in the Essence, the end of the first journey and the beginning of the second. The “hidden” is when the separate self disappears in the divine reality. The “most hidden” is passing beyond awareness of both ways the separate self disappears. In this way the circle of sainthood is completed, the second journey ends, and the traveler no longer experiences this disappearance of the separate self.

The traveler then begins the third journey: from God to creation, through God. They travel through the levels of divine action. As this state passes, full awareness returns, and the traveler remains through God. They travel through the worlds of divine power, spirit, and human life, and witness these worlds themselves and what follows from them.

They receive a share in prophecy: they make known what they have learned about God's essence, attributes, and acts. But theirs is not the kind of prophecy that brings religious law. They speak only of God, His attributes, and His acts, and are not called prophets. They receive religious laws and teachings from the universal Prophet and follow him.

When the third journey ends, the traveler begins the fourth: from creation to God, through God. They study created things, their effects and implications, and learn what benefits or harms them in this life and the next. They learn how all things return to God, how they are guided or driven, and what humiliates, hinders, or helps them. They call people toward God and so become prophets through prophecy. Through the prophecy that brings religious law, they are called prophets. They announce how created things will fare, what harms and benefits them, and what makes them happy or miserable. In all this they act through God, for their existence is rooted in God. Attention to creation does not distract them from attending to Him.

This means the world of God's command, the realm of intellects and spirits. The name comes from Qur'anic expressions such as “Surely creation and command are His” and “Say: the spirit belongs to my Lord's command.” These beings are described this way because they come to exist by God's command without an intervening material process or passage of time. Their basic capacity to exist is enough for them to receive existence; they do not require the special readiness of matter. Their individual independence is also absorbed into that command, so there is no separate recipient giving orders or obeying them, only God's commands.

Anyone who considers the matter will see that what makes a thing what it is comes from its form, not its matter. The world now understood by the intellect will one day be a world directly present, as wide as the heavens and earth, when the sky is rolled up like a written scroll and the heavens are folded in God's right hand.

Doing good includes putting both outward behaviour and inner character in order, letting go of faults, taking on virtues, and ultimately letting the separate self fall away. One can describe this in four stages. First, make outward conduct clear and sound by following divine guidance. Second, remove bad qualities such as greed, envy, and pride, along with the wrongs done by tongue, appetite, and sexual desire. The Prophet is reported to have said: “Whoever is spared the evil of his laqlaq, qabqab, and dhabdhāb has been spared all evil.” These words mean the tongue, the belly, and the penis, respectively. Third, take on noble qualities, described here as reflecting God's names and attributes and developing qualities worthy of God. Fourth comes the loss of self-centredness, described in three degrees: one's actions cease to be regarded as independent of God's action; one's qualities cease to be independent of God's qualities; and one's very existence is understood as having no independence from God's existence.
“Pattern” here means a model or style. To say that something follows a certain pattern means that it is made or ordered in the same way.

The first “where” asks about our origin: “God was, and nothing was with Him.” The third asks about our final destination: “To your Lord is the return,” and “Everything passes away except His face.” The first points to the downward arc of creation: “Go down from here, all of you.” The third points to the upward journey: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord.” The first can also point to the withdrawal or concealment of divine light: God is said to be hidden from created eyes by His radiance, and a tradition speaks of seventy thousand veils of light and seventy thousand of darkness. The verses about the Night of Decree describe the angels and spirit descending by God's permission until dawn. The third direction points to the appearance of light: “God is the light of the heavens and earth.” Another verse speaks of the angels and the spirit ascending to Him on a day measured as fifty thousand years. The second “where” concerns our present life, the time of traveling through the world, looking carefully at it and reflecting on God's signs: “Travel through the earth and see,” and “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that He is the Truth.” God speaks the truth.

Someone might object: “A thing cannot be described as many unless we treat it mathematically, because few and many are properties of number. We call time many only because it can be divided into days and hours. Being many is like being equal or unequal; all depend on quantity.”

The answer is that we call something many once we consider it as a number. But number is not studied only in mathematics. It can be considered in two ways, as the author will explain later. That is why he calls this one way of considering it “mathematical.” In any case, multiplicity has no existence beyond the weak existence it has as a number. As the author will say repeatedly, existence goes together with unity—or may even be one and the same as unity.

The study of nature was divided into eight branches. It studies natural bodies as they change. It may study them in general, in what is called physics or the study of nature. The name of this branch means the first thing one hears when studying nature. It examines such basic matters as time, place, boundaries, movement, and rest.

Natural philosophy may study simple bodies as a whole. This branch is called the study of the heavens and the world. It examines the simple bodies and the wisdom behind how they are made and arranged. Or it may study how simple bodies change into one another. This is the study of things coming into being and passing away. It explains how things are produced and how they reproduce, and how God's care allows earthly bodies to benefit from the rays of the heavens as they grow and live. It also explains how kinds of things continue even though individual things perish through the movements of the heavens.

Another branch studies what happens in the upper air, such as clouds, rain, snow, thunder, lightning, rainbows, and halos. The remaining branches study minerals, plants, animals, and the soul. Minerals are mixed bodies that do not grow or perceive. Plants grow but do not perceive. Animals grow and perceive but do not reason. The soul has all these powers, including reason. Books also list branches of the highest philosophy and of mathematics and the study of nature.
The author sometimes says “existence” and sometimes “existent” to mean the same thing, because what truly exists is existence itself.
The author follows an earlier way of dividing questions, but that division does not simply sort them into “yes” and “no.” Nor is he pointing to the reason for asking a question or its nearest cause.

A clearer way to make the point is this. First, we must answer the skeptic who doubts or denies reality itself by establishing that something exists. Once we do that, we accept that many things exist. We also know that we can make mistakes: we may take something nonexistent to be real, or fail to recognize something that is real. So our first need is to tell what exists from what does not, and to build our thinking and knowledge on that distinction.

We can do this only by studying what can be said about existence as a whole: both the features it shares generally and those that belong to particular kinds of things. For example, we may say that existence itself is real, while a thing's nature is not existence; that existence has different degrees of strength; and that a thing that exists may either have to exist or may depend on something else. What depends on something else may be a substance (a thing in its own right) or a quality.

What does not exist has no place among real things. So the divisions of what exists, and the rules that apply to those divisions, all belong to existence as a whole. The claims made in each science describe features of the things it studies; in the end, those claims are rooted in existence itself. In truth, these inquiries return to the divisions of existence and to the features of its different forms.

That is why first philosophy studies the primary divisions of existence, such as what must exist and what may exist, and what is one or many. It also studies the next divisions, including the subjects of other sciences, considered as things that exist. This also shows why other sciences depend on first philosophy to establish that their subjects exist, unless that is already clear. — ط مد

Someone may ask: If the concepts “existence” and “thing” are shared features that apply to existing realities, why can’t existence itself be defined by description? By “description,” the commentator means a logical description: defining something through an incidental feature drawn from the realm of essences. Clearly, existence has no description of that kind. Also, reality itself can enter the mind only through a concept, so this would amount to defining a thing by itself. The concept of “thing” is just as familiar—or unfamiliar—as the thing it names, while a definition must be clearer than what it defines. — س ره

Someone may object that lacking a definition means lacking a cause that makes a thing what it is, but does not mean lacking a cause of its existence. And the absence of a proof depends on the absence of all four kinds of cause. The answer is that the author has already said that everything except God has a composite structure of matter and form. Lacking a cause that makes it what it is—even if that cause is matter and form in the mind—therefore means lacking a cause of its existence too. When he says in The Beginning and the Return, “Since it has no definition and no cause, it has no proof,” he is reinforcing this answer to the objection. It is also enough simply to deny that existence has a definition; there is no contradiction.

A second objection appeals to the real existence of a possible thing: existence itself has no definition, yet the existence of a possible thing can be proved because it is caused in its very nature. The answer is that if we mean existence simply as existence, it has neither definition nor proof. If we mean existence with a qualification, then it can have both.

A third objection asks: If what has no definition cannot be proved, how can one thing be proved by another when neither causes the other? For example: every human can laugh, and everyone who can laugh can write. Laughter and writing are not causes of one another; both result from a third cause. The answer is that philosophers who study the divine use “proof” in a strict sense for proof from cause to effect. Avicenna says in the Metaphysics of The Healing: “It has no definition and no proof; rather, it is the proof of everything, though clear signs point to it.” That is why they say things with causes can be known only through their causes. If a logician also uses “proof” for reasoning from an effect, that is a broader use of the word. And in the case where two effects share a third cause, we really reason from one effect to that cause, then from the cause to the other effect we want to establish. In the example, we move from laughter to the rational soul, then from the rational soul to the human capacity to write. The proof thus ultimately proceeds through a cause. — س ره

In a definition, “parts” means the elements that make it up. In a proof, it means the middle steps that connect the premises to the conclusion. Their correspondence is considered in light of the material being discussed. — ه ره

A thing’s being itself is necessary. But we still need to distinguish the concept of the thing from the thing itself, as we do in a definition and what it defines; otherwise, we would end up predicating a thing of itself. — س ره

There is a strict sense of “related,” in which it means the relation itself, and a looser, common sense, in which it means the thing that has a relation. The same distinction applies to “universal.” Strictly speaking, the real existent is existence itself; in common usage, “existent” means the essence to which existence belongs. — ه ره

That is, the feature belongs to existence without needing any additional qualifying condition. This is also what it means for existence to be suited, in itself, to receive that feature. Nothing can come between the subject and its feature, not even something equal to the subject, and the feature must apply to the whole subject. If it applied only to a narrower kind, the subject would need an added qualification before it could receive that feature. If it applied more broadly, the qualification would serve no purpose. This also shows why the division must cover every case: otherwise, one of its branches would be narrower than the subject and would not be an essential feature of it. — ط

As explained above, if a feature belongs essentially to a subject, the division must cover every case. The reverse is true only in some cases: a complete division does not always mean that its members are essential features. — ط

As explained above, shared features must be defined as features that apply to existence as a whole, either by themselves or together with their opposite in a complete division. Here, “opposite” means the alternatives that result when something is divided. This resolves the objections the author has raised. — ط

Limiting each science to the study of the essential features of its subject is not just a matter of convention. It is required by proof in sciences that rely on proof, as explained in the logical study of demonstration.

A proof aims to give certainty, so its premises must be certain. Certainty means knowing that something is so and that it cannot be otherwise. A certain premise must therefore be necessary in truth, even if it is possible in the modal sense; otherwise its opposite would remain possible and there would be no certainty. It must be true at every time; otherwise it might be false at some time, leaving the opposite possible. It must be universal across circumstances; otherwise it might be false in some cases, again leaving the opposite possible. Its predicate must also belong to its subject itself: when the subject is affirmed, the predicate is affirmed with it, and when the subject is denied, the predicate is denied, setting everything else aside. This is why an essential predicate must be equal in scope to its subject. If it were narrower—for example, being prone to wonder in relation to animal—simply being an animal would not be enough for that feature to apply. If it were broader, as walking is in relation to human, the qualification “human” would add nothing to the feature’s application.

Because an essential predicate belongs to its subject necessarily, the subject helps explain why the predicate exists. It must therefore appear in the full definition of that predicate. This is the rule for recognizing an essential feature. If a predicate has another predicate, and that predicate has one more, the original subject must appear in the definition of each, all the way down the chain. Each feature is essential to the original subject as well as to the subject of its own proposition. For example, a human being is capable of wonder, can laugh, and shows the teeth when laughing. The same rule applies in the other direction: if a subject has a subject, that first subject must be included in the definitions all the way back. For example, blackness is a visible quality; visible quality is a sensible quality; sensible quality is a quality; quality belongs to essence; and essence is something that exists.

If a predicate is narrower than its subject, that predicate and its opposite in a complete division together form one essential predicate of the broader subject. Each side is essential to the corresponding part of that subject. For example, what exists is divided into what must exist and what may exist. In the definition of either part, the broader subject is included; in the definition of the combined division, the broader subject itself is included. A science, then, is a set of propositions whose subjects share one subject, which appears in the definitions of the subjects and predicates of its questions. This chain begins with a proposition about the science’s broad subject and ends with a proposition whose predicate no longer includes that subject in its definition. The highest branch of philosophy studies body as something that exists; the study of nature begins with body as a natural kind, not merely as something that exists. Likewise, philosophy studies the circle as something that exists, while mathematics studies it as a geometric shape.

These points establish eight things. First, a science is a collection of propositions about one subject, which appears in the definitions of the subjects and predicates of its questions. Second, every science must have a subject shared by its propositions. Third, that subject is what the science examines through its essential features. Fourth, an essential feature belongs to a thing in itself and can be recognized because the thing appears in its definition. Sometimes the subject and predicate are reversed, so the rule is that either the subject appears in the predicate’s definition or the predicate appears in the subject’s definition. For example, what exists is divided into one and many; and what must exist exists. Fifth, an essential predicate does not apply through an intermediary feature—whether that intermediary is broader, narrower, or equal in scope. An intermediary here means something included in the predicate’s definition without the subject itself being included. For example, blackness belongs to a crow through its feathers. Sixth, the predicate must match the subject in scope: it cannot be broader or narrower. Seventh, the predicate in any question must be essential both to the subject of that question and to the subject of the science as a whole. Eighth, sciences differ according to their subjects.

These rules apply to sciences that prove their claims. There is no reason to suppose they apply in the same way to conventional disciplines whose subjects are constructed ideas rather than things that exist in reality. — ط

This note explains the statement that a science studies the essential features of its subject. An essential feature truly belongs to a thing, without metaphor or error. In Arabic grammar, it is a description of the thing itself, not a description of something merely related to it. Put another way, it has no intermediary in how it belongs to the thing. There are different kinds of intermediary, however. A ship’s motion, for example, is an intermediary for the motion of someone sitting on it; not every kind of intermediary works this way. The author discusses these distinctions later, in connection with the primacy of existence.

The features of a distinguishing feature are also features of its general kind because, when the general kind is considered without restriction, it is united with that distinguishing feature. Their features are therefore the same in reality. The features of the intellects, for example, truly belong to existence as existence when existence is considered without qualification. This differs from the features of a body considered as changing: matter and motion are what make it a subject for the study of nature. A body considered simply as something that exists, or as composed of matter and form, is instead a subject for the highest branch of philosophy.

Many later scholars found this difficult. Al-Khwansari, for example, wrote in his notes on The Healing that discussing something narrower than a science’s subject is done only for convenience, because the narrower thing is one kind or class of it. Remember, though, that the older definition of an essential feature—as an external predicate that belongs to something in itself or through something equal to it—can be understood correctly. “In itself” does not mean that the thing causes the feature or necessitates it; that reading would make it hard to explain features of narrower kinds. It means that no intermediary stands between the thing and the feature, and that the feature belongs to the thing itself rather than to something merely related to it.

An equal thing here means a concept equal to the subject in the respect under discussion, even if the two concepts differ. Unity and existence, for example, are different concepts but apply to the same reality. If indivisibility belongs to existence because of unity, it is still an essential feature. Likewise, if existence cannot be truly applied to many things because of individuality, that too is an essential feature. But two things may be equal in what exists while belonging to different qualifying aspects. If one feature belongs to a subject only through another aspect attached to it, it is incidental, just as a feature that belongs through something narrower would be. That is why earlier thinkers spoke broadly of a property beyond a thing’s definition, including properties considered with an added qualification. Otherwise, unity, being a thing, possibility, and other features grasped by reason would be left out. — س ره

Here are examples from the study of nature. An essential feature of its main subject is that every body has a natural shape. An essential feature of one kind is that one element changes into another. A general feature of a kind is that an element is in motion. An essential feature of a kind of essential feature is that the lights of the heavens stimulate plant life. A general feature of that kind is that the lights of the heavens, especially the sun, warm the world of the elements. In the last two examples, the feature stays within the scope of the subject of the science. — س ره

The statement made from a general kind and its distinguishing feature is a particular claim: “Some animals are rational.” This shows that the distinguishing feature belongs to the relevant share of the general kind, not to the general kind as such. The claim that a kind’s essential or incidental features belong to its general kind is rejected, for the reasons already given. — ط مد

A careful reader should see that a feature attached to something narrower—such as a particular subject in a science narrower than the highest branch of philosophy—can in one respect be essential to the broader subject and in another respect incidental. The reason is that a general kind has its own reality at the level of the concept and its reality in the world, and these are far apart. When the broader subject and narrower subject are one in the world but not at the level of the concept, a feature of the narrower subject is incidental to the broader concept but essential to the broader thing in reality. This resolves the difficulty. What matters for a feature to be essential is that no intermediary lies between it and its subject. But we may consider the subject as it is at the level of a concept or as it is in reality, and the judgment changes accordingly. This creates no contradiction for a clear-minded reader. — ن ره

The argument shows that existing things differ in degree. It does not show that the parts we imagine within the concept of existence differ in degree. Strictly speaking, it is real existence that has degrees; its concept does so only indirectly. This is what is meant when the author says that existence is a general concept applied to things by degrees. — ط

Be aware—may God guide us both—that Aristotle's followers, philosophers of illumination, and other careful thinkers do not seriously disagree that the natural universal exists. Philosophers call it “essence”; mystical writers call it the “fixed reality”; different schools use other names for it. By “natural universal,” I do not mean an essence considered without restriction, whose existence is only in the mind and is a mental construct. I mean the underlying essence that can be considered as absolute, combined with conditions, or separate from matter. This underlying essence is even harder to grasp than “absolute essence,” one of its divisions. How could it fail to exist if the combined essence is one of its divisions? That alone is enough to establish the point.

There is no need to use the older argument that the natural universal exists because it is a part of a composite essence. An essence considered without restriction is not literally a part of an essence considered together with a condition; only an essence considered specifically apart from other conditions is a part. If Avicenna meant by “without restriction” the essence as it exists within what is considered apart from other conditions, his part-and-whole argument would work: it would establish the general essence from matter itself. But the argument I have given from the combined essence is already enough. There is also no need for Lahiji's explanation that the “part” in this argument is merely a part in thought.

The real dispute is whether, once a cause brings an essence about, the essence exists in its own right and existence is what lets us affirm it, or whether the essence is called existent only because existence is a feature that belongs to it. There are three kinds of such attribution. First, something may be described as moving only because something connected to it moves, as when we say a passenger moves because the ship moves; in truth, the passenger is not the source of that motion. Second, a subject may truly have a feature, as when a body is black because of its blackness. Both the body and blackness exist, and the body is genuinely black, though it can exist without being black. Third, a general kind and its distinguishing feature may form one reality: the general kind cannot exist without the distinguishing feature.

The view that existence is fundamental is not like the first case, since the natural universal truly exists; its existence is not merely figurative. Nor is it exactly like the second, since a body can exist without blackness, while an essence has no actual existence apart from existence. It is closer to the third case, though with a difference: the existence of a species is attributed to its general kind, its distinguishing feature, and the complete species made from both; the relation between essence and existence is more like that between a shadow and what casts it.

Both sides agree that when we say an essence exists, we must explain what makes it real and in what respect we are calling it existent. An essence by itself is open to both existence and nonexistence. If the only qualifying factor were the mental idea of existence, or a merely conceptual relation to the cause—as those who have not seen this clearly claim—then the essence would still not be real. Adding one mental concept to another does not create an existing thing. The concept of existence is itself just an idea; it is “existence” by its definition, not because it exists as a separate thing in the world. The same applies to the idea of “necessary existence.” By contrast, the illuminating relation is itself the light of existence, just as real bringing-into-existence is actual existence. In that light, the different expressions point to one reality. This shows why accusing the author of assuming what he is trying to prove is mistaken.

There is another reason the accusation fails. The author's point is that reality is an essence taken together with existence. Without existence, an essence is not yet real. So how could existence itself fail to be real when it is what makes an essence real? — س ره

The author means that the outside world is where the existence of existence is found, not that the outside world is a container for existence itself; that latter question is not at issue here. We infer that external things are where existence's own existence is found. If existence is present in something else because it is received in it, then it is even more fitting for it to be present in itself, since nothing can be separate from itself. — ن ره

In a proof, “existent” means whatever has existence, whether a thing's being itself—which means it cannot be separated from itself—or its being something else. This is what “existent” and similar derived words mean in the language of reasoned proof, which aims to grasp things as they are in reality, whether or not everyday language uses the words in exactly the same way. It is simply a matter of terminology. — ن ره
The passage quoted here from The Healing was confused in places, so we have reproduced it from the original source.

If we included the kind of thing described in the distinguishing feature itself, the species would become part of its own distinguishing feature. This is an even stronger objection than the one given afterward. Someone could challenge that later objection by saying that it is not really a case of a thing being affirmed of itself. But this would not affect the claim that a merely possible statement would become necessary: its logical status would still be necessity.

Here is the point. In the statement, the predicate may be the whole qualified expression, “human,” with the qualification outside it but included in the way the predicate is restricted. Then “human” is what is directly being said of the subject, and the statement is necessary. Or the predicate may be “human” with the qualification included in it. In that case the qualification is considered only indirectly; the main point is still that the subject is human. Compare “Zayd is in the house,” where his location is the point, with “Zayd is standing in the house,” where the location is secondary. The statement “a human is a human who can laugh” contains two claims: “a human is a human,” which is necessary, and “a human can laugh,” which is possible. This is like the way philosophers analyze the subject phrase in a statement: Avicenna treats it as unrestricted, while al-Farabi treats it as possible. It is also established that before we know a description, it functions as a report; once we know it, a report can function as a description.

Another argument that the thing itself is not built into a derived adjective is that describing a cloth as white does not repeat the subject, either generally or in a narrower sense. If the word “white” included the thing it describes, the subject would be repeated. — س ره

A derived adjective has one simple descriptive meaning; it is not made up of the adjective plus the thing it describes. Because it is descriptive, however, it needs a link to its subject, supplied by the pronoun. — ن ره

The commentator gives two reasons for the view that a feature and the thing described by it are one. First, when we see something white, what we directly perceive is whiteness. Before considering the theory that whiteness is a feature that cannot exist on its own, we naturally call it both whiteness and white. If whiteness and “white” were not one in reality, we could not make that judgment so readily. Second, Aristotle and the translators of his work use derived adjectives to name the categories. If those adjectives were not one with the things they describe in reality, this usage and these examples would require an awkward explanation: we would have to say that the adjectives merely point to the underlying features. — س ره

The soul is pure being because what lies above it, and the goal of its perfection, are pure being too. It also has no fixed limit at which it stops. And each concept, such as “immaterial substance,” is itself, not an “I.” — س ره
Here “essence” means what makes a thing what it is, as the words that follow show. The source uses the noun where a pronoun would normally appear. — س ره

Someone might say that this argument assumes what it is trying to prove. The answer is that it leaves out a step: otherwise, the essential features would not differ. That is the difficulty the author is pointing to. — س ره

The view that limits the rule to cases other than simple claims of existence is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's. Replacing “depends on” with “implies” is the view of Jalal al-Din al-Dawani. The claim that existence is not attributed to an essence even in the mind, and has no individual instance until it belongs to an essence, is held by a later scholar known as the meticulous Sayyid. This resembles the author's claim that the concept of “human” is united with a human being's own particular reality, even though the concept itself is not what exists outside the mind. The Sayyid reverses the claim: for him, the concept of existence has nothing corresponding to it in reality. To say that a thing is united with a concept means that the thing itself, without qualification, is represented by and drawn from that concept. — س ره

By “its own reality,” the author means existence without limiting it to one particular degree. He does not mean only the highest degree. Existence has levels. Imagine them rising from weak to strong, then from strong to stronger still. Each lower level is limited because it lacks some of what the next higher level possesses. The higher level, in turn, contains the completeness of the lower. Yet each higher level is itself limited in relation to one above it. This continues until we reach a level with no limit at all—its only limit is that it has none. This is pure reality taken with the condition that it be considered apart from other levels, making it one level among them. Taken without that condition, it would include all the levels and would not be one level opposed to the rest. — ط

The author chooses “particularization” here instead of “individuality,” as he also does in The Divine Witnesses, to point to a subtle idea: existence is one reality that unfolds through different forms and states. In a hierarchy of levels, existences are distinct through their own priority or posteriority. Being prior is part of what an existence is, though not in the way a part belongs to a whole. The concept “priority,” by contrast, is a relation and does not make up the existence itself. In a series of things at the same level, that concept necessarily follows and does not arise later than existence. A thing may also be distinguished by material features when it exists in matter.

To see how features can make a thing distinct, consider the difference between an adjective and the underlying feature named by it. When “black” is considered as a description of a subject, it is an adjective that applies to the subject. When “blackness” is considered on its own, it is a feature that the subject bears. The difference depends on how we consider them. A similar distinction applies when we consider a body without qualification or as something set apart from what belongs to it. Features distinguish a thing in the first sense because they share one existence with their subject; a thing becomes distinct through its particular way of existing. In the second sense, the feature is not predicated of the subject in the same way and does not share its existence. The feature exists for the subject, rather than being the subject’s own existence, so it comes after the subject exists. How could it make the subject distinct before that? We may still call such features signs of distinctness. In the first sense they are necessary consequences of the thing; in the second, their being necessary while separate from the subject is harder to explain. That is why philosophers treated certain quantities, qualities, and positions as necessary features.

The alternatives here rule out only the possibility that neither applies; they need not exclude one another. Another possibility is that the intellects have no essence. The earlier either-or should be understood in the same way. This is why the second division has two branches: in the different degrees of existence, what makes them distinct is also what they share. — س ره

The point is that existence is one reality, one kind, whose degrees and essences differ without being separated by distinct essential features, as different universal essences are. Across these degrees, what makes existences different is the same as what makes them one. This reveals the meaning of Imam Ali's saying: “His unity is His distinction from His creation; distinction means a difference in quality, not separation into isolation.” The absence of isolating separation is the secret of existence as one reality. Understand this, if you are ready for it: here lies the highest aim. — ن ره

Someone may ask: How can essences distinguish existences if essences are not established before existence? On the view that existence is fundamental, existences themselves have no prior independent reality either. The first answer is that essences need not come before existence or be fundamental in their own right. It is enough for different essences to arise together with existence. An essence is real only in a secondary sense, because existence is real; it is made only in a secondary sense, because existence is what is made. Think of colored light appearing at the same time as colored glass is formed. Second, essences may be prior in what they are. Third, they may have earlier forms of existence, so their differences in an earlier realm can distinguish existences in a later one. Ultimately, the explanation reaches the fixed realities linked to God's names and attributes at the level of divine oneness. These are not made, and neither are their differences; this is where the question of what caused the differences comes to an end. — س ره

The self-evident general idea of existence is a mental construct; it has no existence outside the mind. It is not like “human,” which exists in the world and also has a mental form. If the concept of existence existed in both ways, then its essence would move between external and mental existence, and actual existence could be in the mind—something the author has already ruled out. As for how the mind can draw this idea from the reality of existence, even though that reality cannot enter the mind and the mind cannot move into the outside world, the author will explain later. This is what he means by saying that the general, self-evident idea of existence then follows in the mind: the mind contains the idea, not the individual realities together with the idea. — ط مد

The question is whether the reality of existence is made from a general kind and a distinguishing feature, as the argument supposes. The author does not discuss the possibility that it is made from something still broader and the third element of a three-part division, since that would obviously lead to an endless chain. Nor can the general kind be broader than both the first and third elements: in the third case, the general kind would not become one of the parts that make up the whole. By “something else,” the author means a species.

In the first case, a distinguishing feature, considered on its own, brings the general kind into actuality. The two then stand as matter and form, with form acting alongside matter to make the whole. Some commentators say that a distinguishing feature causes only certain qualities of a general kind, such as its ability to exist in a particular form or to be definite. But since the general kind also causes some qualities of the distinguishing feature, the argument instead makes the feature a cause of the very essence of the general kind. That would contradict the assumption that existence's reality is their composite whole.

In the second case, what makes broader kind and species the same in reality would also have to be what makes them different. General kind, distinguishing feature, and species are different ideas but one reality, as predication requires. Here, however, the idea of the distinguishing feature and the idea of the species are both identical with the reality of existence. So none of them could really be a broader kind, a feature that distinguishes it, or a species. Existence could not be composed of them. This reasoning establishes both that existences are simple realities and that existence itself is not a general kind. — س ره
What makes the elements one would have to be the very thing that makes them different. — ن ره

This argument takes an unnecessarily long route. If existence were a general kind, its species would either be a kind of existence, in which case everything in question is already existence, or an essence of some other kind. In the first case, there is no need to prove from the general kind that the species or its distinguishing feature is existence. In the second, what needs to be shown is that the species is existence. The author's wording suggests that he thinks the opponent is claiming that the general kind “existence” is predicated of its distinguishing feature. Perhaps that is what the opponent means. If the argument said “general kind” where it says “distinguishing feature,” the difficulty would be even clearer. A general kind is indeterminate by nature, while a distinguishing feature and a species are definite. Form is what makes a thing what it is, just as a distinguishing feature is what makes a species what it is. But this brings us back to the first argument given by the author and by Avicenna in the Metaphysics of The Healing. — س ره

If the distinguishing feature is predicated of its general kind, as in “some animals are rational,” then one might have to say “some existence is not existence.” The author gives this as a counterexample. The answer is that a general kind is a broad feature in relation to its distinguishing feature, just as the distinguishing feature is a specific feature in relation to the general kind. A feature that distinguishes existence could itself be called existence without becoming a species under existence; the predication is incidental. — س ره
They fall under substance only incidentally, just as a thing can be classed under a necessary property it implies, even though that property is not part of what the thing is. — ه ره
See Stage Four, in the chapter on how the general kind is taken from matter and the distinguishing feature from form. — ه ره
The relation between an individual and its species is like the relation between a distinguishing feature and its general kind. — ه ره

This means a species considered under its general kind. The author begins with species rather than general kind to show that a part of a general kind needs a distinguishing feature. The general idea of a species relates to its particular instances as parents relate to their children—not as one parent relates to all the children. — س ره

You may think the author should say that the other three kinds of universal idea reduce only to species, or else add “distinguishing feature” as well. If he means universals that apply to many things with the same underlying nature, they reduce to species. If he follows the common account, in which a shared feature reduces to a general kind and a defining feature to a distinguishing feature, then “distinguishing feature” should be added. The answer may be that he follows the second account but does not name the distinguishing feature because it is only part of a complete nature; the whole nature is the species, so naming the species is enough. The general kind, too, is only an incomplete part, but its breadth makes it relevant when discussing shared features. More likely, the author follows the first account: the other three universal ideas are all treated as species because they are complete. A distinguishing feature is only part of a nature, though the species becomes what it is through that feature. As Avicenna says, “A thing's form is its reality, that by which it is what it is.” The other three kinds of universal apply to many individual things with the same underlying nature. A general kind, by contrast, is only an indeterminate part of a nature. In reality, it is an open choice among distinguishing features, an ambiguity that moves among species. What the mind pictures as a complete, definite thing is actually matter considered apart from its form, not a general kind. It has no individual cases sharing one complete nature—especially at the highest levels of general kinds, and in the highest general kinds of qualities, which are simple realities. This is why the author does not reduce it to a species. — س ره

This is like a general kind and distinguishing feature, considered as what is still vague and what makes it definite; or like existence and nonexistence, as in complete, separate intellects. Dividing a thing into parts in either way makes it dependent on those parts. Consider this carefully. — ن ره

The relation here is like a shadow to what casts it, or a reflection to the surface that reflects it—not like one independent thing attaching to another. Existence is not one item in a series that could be followed by another existence. If we imagine a second existence alongside pure existence, that second would be the same as the first. Existence is light, and things are its rays; existence is the root, and everything else is a branch of it. — ن ره

The author says the resulting identity is “distinct from” the First, rather than merely saying its concept differs from the concept of existence, to point to a subtle idea: existence is the very act of proceeding from the First and being related to it. Dependence on another is part of what dependent existence is, as explained earlier. — س ره

What necessarily follows from something is made real through the very act that makes its basis real; it is not made by a second act. The same applies to what is not made. The scholar's statement therefore clearly supports the view that existence is what is made real. This truth even appears in the writing of a determined defender of the view that essences are fundamental, al-Lahiji. In the twenty-seventh question of The Dawning Lights, he says that calling essence what is made means only that we should not imagine essences fixed in nonexistence before they are made, with existence or the condition of existing added afterward. Once that mistaken idea is removed, there is no problem in saying that existence—or the fact that something exists—is what is made, since no essence exists before it is made. — س ره
Even if essences detached from all existence could somehow exist, the nature of a general kind would still come before the nature of a species. That is priority in the very nature of a thing. — س ره

The point is that considering an essence stripped of every kind of existence and every other feature does not, by itself, give it existence. It removes all existence and all features from it. Only when we add a second thought—that this very stripping is itself a kind of mental existence—does the question of existence arise. Even then, there is no problem or endless chain: the sequence ends when the mind stops considering it. We can also say that stripping essence is itself a kind of “mixing” with the idea of stripping, not with actual existence, so no further act of stripping is needed. This is like saying that prime matter is the potential for form and other things in a body. If we then ask whether this potential itself has actual existence, we might imagine an endless series of potentials and actualities. The answer is that the actuality of the potential is the potential itself, not something added to it—just as parts of time do not need another time in order to be earlier or later. In short, essence is stripped of existence when considered in its primary sense; it is mixed with existence only in the common, expanded sense. In the first sense, it is not described as existing, so the question of how it can be described that way does not arise. The author says it is described as existing under one consideration only to grant the objection for the sake of argument. — س ره

A statement can be analyzed into three parts—the subject, the idea of the predicate, and the predicate's being affirmed of the subject—when we examine its concepts. That does not mean these three parts all exist in reality. In “Zayd is Zayd,” we can distinguish three conceptual parts, but the reality of the statement is just the subject itself. The author has another answer in one of his treatises. Existence exists through itself, while an essence exists through existence. So “the human being exists” means that existence is what makes the idea of humanity true in the outside world. In reality, the idea of “human” is affirmed of this existence and depends on it, as a shadow depends on what casts it. This applies when we mean a particular reality. If we mean the general concept of existence, it works like other mental features: they apply to things once those things are established or distinguished in the mind. But the broad mental idea of existence is not what makes an essence real and removes nonexistence from it; like other mental concepts, it is outside the essence of everything. — س ره
